Free for all Tally users, no coding needed","content":"Conditional logic lets your form adapt in real time based on how someone answers. Show or hide questions, skip irrelevant pages, jump to a custom thank you page, or route respondents down a completely different path — all based on their responses. The result is a smarter, shorter form that feels personal instead of generic.
Conditional logic in Tally is completely free to use. No upgrade needed, no limits on the number of conditions you can add.
Conditional logic is a versatile tool that allows you to create tailored form experiences based on user responses. Some examples of using conditional logic include:
- Progressive disclosure: Only show fields when they're needed. Use this for waiting list forms, client check-in forms, or any form where follow-up questions depend on a previous answer.
- Lead qualification: Ask progressively detailed questions and end the form early if someone doesn't qualify — no wasted time for you or them. Route high-intent leads to a specific page or redirect URL.
- Pricing calculators: Use calculated fields with conditional logic to display custom quotes, totals, or estimates based on selections — updated live as respondents answer.
- Personalized confirmation: Show a different thank you page or message based on how someone answered — useful for quiz results, NPS follow-ups, or application outcomes.
- Personality quizzes: Display the result category respondents scored highest on, using calculated fields and conditional page jumps. See how in the personality quiz guide.
Type 
/logic to add conditional logic to your form. You can add conditions on any type of input block. Click 
: next to the logic block to remove, duplicate, add new, or wrap conditions in a group.
Use the 
cmd/ctrl + shift + L shortcut to add a conditional logic block under a selected input block.
When a logic block has more than one condition, use the 
When dropdown to choose how they're combined. - When all match: every condition must be true (an AND rule). Use this to narrow down to a specific combination of answers, for example, respondents from "Germany" who are older than 18.
- When any match: at least one condition must be true (an OR rule). Use this when several different answers should trigger the same result, for example, someone who selected "Consulting" or "Freelance" as their job type.
Nesting condition groups
Click 
⋮ next to a condition to wrap it in a group. Each group has its own all/any setting, so you can combine rules like "(Age is under 18) AND (Country is Germany OR France)" by nesting an "any" group inside an "all" group.
After adding a conditional logic block to your form, you can select from six types of actions to trigger. You’ll find them in the 
Then dropdown.Jump to page enables you to skip pages with questions that don't concern your respondents or to redirect them to a different Thank you page. In the example below, the 
Jump to page is configured to redirect respondents under 18 to page 3 rather than continuing with the rest of the form flow.
It’s important to place the conditional logic block on the page where you want the jump action to trigger. The jump will only trigger when respondents click the “Next” or “Submit” button.
Renaming your pages makes it easier to identify your pages when installing page jumps in a lengthy form with a lot of pages. You can rename a page by clicking the page number.
When working on a long form, a content table on the right side of the builder lets you jump between pages and fields instantly. It appears automatically once your form has 12 or more fields.
With calculated fields, you can use your respondents' answers to calculate (and display) scores, prices, or other values.
The 
Require answer option allows you to set a form field as required or not, depending on the respondent's input. For example, if a respondent wants to sign up for your newsletter, make the email input field required.
You can use the keyboard shortcut to make selected questions required:
ctrl/cmd + shift + R
You can show or hide any block in your form depending on your respondents’ answers.
How to hide blocks with conditional logic
Insert 
Conditional logic and choose Hide blocks. Click the small arrow (▸) next to a page or question name to expand it and select individual blocks inside.  If you select a page name directly (without expanding), all blocks on that page will be selected.
Use the keyboard shortcut to hide selected blocks: 
ctrl/cmd + shift + H
How to show blocks with conditional logic
To show blocks conditionally, you need to hide them first. Click 
⋮⋮ to open block settings and click Hide. When you click a question title, all answer options are selected automatically.
Then, insert 
Conditional logic and choose Show blocks . Use the dropdown to select the blocks you want to show. Selecting a page or a question will select all blocks inside that page or question. Using 
Hide button to disable completion, you can prevent respondents from submitting your form by hiding the submit button or the button to proceed to the next page.
You can redirect respondents to different websites, landing pages, or Tally forms upon form completion. For this, you’ll need to use conditional logic and calculated fields.
You can also add hidden blocks to allow respondents to enter additional information before leaving the form for more comprehensive and trackable lead capture. As a result, the form creates an interactive landing page-like experience. 
When dealing with long forms, conditional logic can become more intricate and prone to logical errors. With extensive fields, conditions, and actions, it's crucial to be cautious, as even small mistakes can sneak in. To effectively troubleshoot your form, you can follow these general steps:
- Review the conditional logic blocks: Start by carefully examining the conditional logic rules you've set up for your form. Check if the conditions are linked to the correct fields and actions. Ensure that you have configured the logic correctly based on your specific requirements.
- Edit field names: Replace the default question field names with descriptive titles that accurately describe the question or information being collected. This will make it easier to identify and manage fields when setting up or troubleshooting conditional logic.
- Test your form: Before sending your form to respondents, test different scenarios. You may find it easier to spot any errors by doing several test runs and selecting different answer options each time.
- Use @ mentions to identify the specific issue: By strategically placing @ mentions before or after the conditional logic block, you create a mechanism to track the values of relevant inputs and calculated fields at specific points in the form's execution.
- Simplify to narrow down the problem: By reducing the complexity of the logic, you can isolate specific conditions or actions that may be causing the issue and focus your efforts on debugging those areas.
What is a conditional logic form?
A conditional logic form is a form that dynamically changes based on how someone answers. Using IF/THEN rules, you can show, hide, or skip questions so each respondent only sees what's relevant to them.
Is Tally's conditional logic free?
Yes. Conditional logic is available for free to all Tally users. There are no limits on the number of conditions you can add.
What types of actions can I trigger with conditional logic?
Tally supports six actions: Jump to page, Calculate a value, Make answers required, Show or hide blocks, Hide button to disable completion, and Redirect to different URLs.
Can I combine conditional logic with multi-step forms?
Absolutely. Conditional logic and multi-step forms work great together. You can skip entire pages, show different paths based on answers, and create personalized form flows.
Why isn't my conditional logic working?
The most common issues are: the logic block is placed on the wrong page, conditions reference the wrong field, or the form hasn't been tested with all answer combinations. Use the troubleshooting steps above to debug.","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_e54d2793c843d152f87f","url":"https://tally.so/help/hidden-fields","title":"Capture data with Hidden fields | Free Form Builder | Tally Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"Add hidden fields to your Tally forms to track traffic sources, pass data with URL parameters, and personalize responses automatically. Free for all users.","content":"You can use URL parameters to pass data into hidden fields in your form. This lets you include information you already have in the form URL, helping you personalize the respondent’s experience and gain more detailed insights from your results.
Hidden fields are available for free to all Tally users.
A hidden field lets you track respondents and use already collected data to personalize your forms. It’s invisible to anyone filling out a form but lets you gather and use data effectively.
Some examples may include:
- Track the traffic source of your respondent (social media, triggers on your website, or other)
- Pass on information about your respondent to your responses (like name or email address)
- Mention information in your form, such as your respondent’s name, using answer piping
- Prefill the input fields on your form
- Pass on UTM parameters to track marketing campaigns
Hidden fields are not the same as hiding a field’s visibility. 
Open your form editor and type 
/hidden to insert a Hidden field block.
Add the hidden fields you want to pass on to your form. You can add as many hidden field blocks as you like. If you want to add your respondent's name and traffic source, add two hidden field blocks and name them, for example, 'name' and 'ref'.
Finish your form and 
Publish it. Find your form’s URL in the share tab.
When you are ready to share the form, add the parameters and corresponding values to your URL before sharing the link. There are two ways to add the parameters:
- Manually: add the variable to your form URL before sharing your form.
- Automated: use any CRM system (such as Salesforce) or email automation tool (such as Mailchimp or ActiveCampaign) to populate your data, so your respondents automatically receive a customized URL with the correct data.
The first hidden field should start with 
? . When adding multiple fields, separate them with & . 
For example, if your respondent’s name is Marie and the traffic source is email, the URL would look like this: https://tally.so/r/nPA50m?name=Marie&ref=email
You will find the hidden fields and corresponding answers in the 
Submissions tab after respondents submit your form.
Read more about mentioning hidden fields in your form using answer piping. You can also add hidden fields to your redirect URL to pass information from one form to another.
To learn about using hidden fields with popular CRM systems and email automation tools, take a look at our guides:","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_8e9aaf6b346405cb077c","url":"https://tally.so/help/form-calculator","title":"Automated Form Calculations | Free Form Builder | Tally Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"Add calculated fields to your Tally forms to score quizzes, set dynamic prices, or assign lead values based on responses. Free and easy to set up today.","content":"Calculated fields let you perform automatic calculations inside your form — think pricing calculators, quiz score totals, or lead scoring, all based on respondents' answers. You can use simple numeric and text operations, or write full formula expressions for more advanced logic.
Calculated fields are available for free to all Tally users. 
Calculated fields enable you to dynamically calculate values based on respondents' answers. Here are some common use cases for calculated fields:
- Pricing calculators: Build a checkout form where the total updates live as respondents choose products, quantities, or add-ons. Feed the result directly into a payment block.
- Quiz scoring: Add points per correct answer and show respondents their final score on a thank you page. See our guide to building scored quizzes.
- Personality and category quizzes: Tally up answers across categories and route respondents to the matching result page. See our personality quiz guide.
- Lead qualification: Assign a score or status label ("Hot lead," "Nurture") based on the answers someone gives, and sync it to your CRM via an integration.
- Name and text concatenation: Combine first name and last name into a single "Full name" field, or build a custom reference string from multiple inputs.
- Conditional redirects that use a calculated field with conditional logic to redirect respondents to different pages based on their responses.
Insert a calculated field in your form by typing 
/calculated field. In most cases, it’s best to add calculated fields on top of the form.
- Name your calculated field to easily retrieve it in calculations later on
- Choose whether the value will be text or a numeric value (number)
- Then, add an initial value as a starting point of your calculation. You can type a value, leave it blank or select a value from the dropdown.
Before determining the value of a calculated field, you need to add conditional logic to your form. Type
/logic to insert it below your calculated field block. Only you can see the calculated field and conditional logic blocks, respondents won’t see them on your published form. Conditional logic allows you to perform multiple actions. When using calculated fields, you want to select the 
Calculate action.
You can perform several numeric and textual operations with the 
Calculate action:
- Add a value
- Subtract a value
- Multiply with a value
- Divide with a value
- Assign: add a text value, for example, a label or a status, to sync contacts from your form submissions with a CRM or another tool or assign a category name to respondents based on their selected answers. Respondents won’t see this information unless it’s mentioned elsewhere in the form.
- Concatenate values: combine values in one string. For example, if you have fields for first name and last name in your form, you can create a calculated field that combines the values entered in these two fields into a single ‘Full name’ field. To use this, you need to select Text when creating a calculated field.
With formulas you write a single expression to combine multiple operations in one go, instead of chaining separate logic steps. Reference any field with 
@ mentions (e.g. (@price * @quantity) - @discount) and get real-time validation as you type.
Supported operations are 
+ - * / and parentheses ( ) for grouping
| Use case | Formula | 
| Add tax (5%) | @price × 1.05 | 
| Total with quantity | @price × @quantity | 
| Price after discount | (@price × @quantity) - @discount | 
| Apply a dynamic discount % (discount set by respondent) | @price × ((100 − @discount) / 100) | 
| Apply a fixed discount % (e.g. always 20% off) | @price × ((100 − 20) / 100) | 
| Remove a dynamic tax rate from a total (tax rate set by respondent) | @total × ((100 − @tax_rate) / 100) | 
| Remove a fixed tax % from a total (e.g. always 16% VAT) | @total × ((100 + 16) / 100) | 
| Calculate a quiz score | @score_q1  + @score_q2  + @score_q3 | 
| Build a URL with text concatenation | "https://example.com/"  + @page | 
| Combine first and last name | @first_name  + " "  + @last_name | 
| Prefix a field with a label | "ORD-"  + @order_id | 
| Build an address string | @street  + ", "  + @city  + ", "  + @country | 
| Make a certificate-style text | @first_name  + " "  + @last_name  + " has completed "  + @course_name | 
Tips:
- Always use @ + autocomplete to insert a form field
- Only type manually if you want to add text or numbers that aren’t collected in the form
- Use parentheses () to control order of operations
- Wrap literal text in double quotes, e.g. "https://example.com/" + @page
Calculations on date blocks are not available yet. 
By default, calculated values are not visible in your form. You can find them in the 
Submissions tab of your form, but you can also display the calculated values in your form, use them in a payment form, or create a dynamic redirect on completion.
To mention the calculated value in your form, simply type 
@ and choose the calculated field from the dropdown menu. You can use this to show a final price, score or quiz result in your form.
If you want to calculate and display currency, add your currency symbol directly before the linked calculated field, like in the example below.
You can use a calculated field to calculate the price of your payment form and make it dynamic based on your respondents’ answers. This means the price will change based on other inputs and logic.
- Type /payment to insert a payment form.
- Choose your calculated field from the Price dropdown menu in your payment block.
- The price will now automatically update according to your respondent's answers, for example, if they select different product types or quantities.
You can redirect respondents to different websites, landing pages, or Tally forms upon form completion. For this, you’ll need to use calculated fields and conditional logic.
You can also add hidden blocks to allow respondents to enter additional information before leaving the form for more comprehensive and trackable lead capture. As a result, the form creates an interactive landing page-like experience. 
You can use calculated fields to customize the email body or recipients of your respondent or self email notifications. Learn more about dynamic email notifications here.
Can I build a calculator with Tally?
Yes, use calculated fields together with conditional logic to build pricing calculators, quiz score counters, lead scoring systems, and more. Calculated fields are free for all users.
What's the difference between numeric operations and formulas?
Numeric operations (add, subtract, multiply, divide) apply one step at a time via conditional logic. Formulas lets you write a single expression combining multiple operations, e.g. 
(price * quantity) - discount.
Can calculated fields be hidden from respondents?
Yes. Calculated fields and conditional logic are only visible to you in the form editor. Respondents only see them if you explicitly 
@ mention the field value somewhere in the form.
I want to display the result on the Thank You page
Use answer piping: type 
@ on your Thank You page and select the calculated field from the dropdown. The respondent will see the final value after submission.
My calculated field always shows 0
This is almost always a placement or logic ordering issue. Check the following:
- The calculated field must be placed BELOW the questions it references. Tally evaluates fields top-to-bottom. If your calculated field appears above a question it references, it can't read that question's value yet. Move the calculated field to after all questions that feed into it.
- Conditional logic must fire before the calculated field is displayed. If you're using conditional logic to show/hide questions, make sure the logic conditions are evaluated before the calculated field block appears in the form flow.
- Test in the published form, not the editor. The editor preview doesn't always reflect real-time calculation. Publish your form (or use the preview link) to see the actual calculated result.
- Check your formula for typos. Field references are case-sensitive. Open the calculated field and confirm each @FieldName matches exactly the question title in your form.
If the score still shows 0 after these checks, try rebuilding the calculated field from scratch, sometimes cached formula state causes issues.
The form jumps to the wrong page
When combining Calculate actions with Jump to page actions, remember that conditional logic is evaluated from top to bottom. If an earlier logic block triggers a page jump, later blocks on the same page won't execute. Place all Calculate actions before any Jump to page actions.","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_7d74204bcd05c7c5bb0d","url":"https://tally.so/help/answer-piping","title":"Answer Piping for Smarter Forms | Free Form Builder | Tally Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"Use answer piping in Tally to mention respondents' previous answers throughout your form. grade.markdown:
# Tally — Form Builder Guide

> Tally is a document-style form builder for creating, publishing, and sharing online forms. It offers unlimited forms and submissions on its free plan, subject to fair usage guidelines; some features require Pro or Business.

You can try building a form without signing up, but Tally’s terms say an account is required to publish it.

Forms can be built from a blank page, a template, an AI prompt, or imported material, including Typeform forms and supported files.

## Choose a starting point

- [Get started](<https://tally.so/help/get-started>): An introduction to creating and publishing a first form.
- [Create a form](<https://tally.so/help/create-a-form>): Build with questions and blocks, then customize, publish, and share.
- [Template gallery](<https://tally.so/templates>): Explore ready-made forms to customize.
- [Create with Tally AI](<https://tally.so/help/free-ai-form-builder>): Generate or edit a form from a plain-language prompt; AI is optional and available on the free plan.
- [Import an existing form](<https://tally.so/help/import>): Bring in Typeform forms or supported files as editable drafts; review them before sharing.
- [Pricing and plan features](<https://tally.so/pricing>): Compare free, Pro, and Business features and check fair-usage qualifications.

## Build and customize

- [Input blocks](<https://tally.so/help/input-blocks>): Choose fields for answers, selections, dates, uploads, payments, and other inputs.
- [Editor shortcuts](<https://tally.so/help/keyboard-shortcuts>): Use slash commands and keyboard shortcuts to insert and arrange blocks.
- [Conditional logic](<https://tally.so/help/conditional-form-logic>): Show or hide blocks, skip pages, and adapt a form to responses.
- [Calculated fields](<https://tally.so/help/form-calculator>): Calculate scores, prices, and other values from answers.
- [Hidden fields](<https://tally.so/help/hidden-fields>): Pass URL parameters into a form for personalization or source tracking.
- [Customize form design](<https://tally.so/help/customize-your-form>): Adjust themes, colors, fonts, images, and layout; custom CSS requires Pro.
- [Multi-page forms](<https://tally.so/help/how-to-create-a-multi-step-form>): Arrange questions across pages or present them one at a time.
- [Use and create templates](<https://tally.so/help/form-templates>): Customize gallery templates or save a published form as a reusable template.

## Publish, collect, and connect

- [Embed a form](<https://tally.so/help/embed-your-form>): Add a published form to a webpage as a standard, popup, or full-page embed.
- [Form settings](<https://tally.so/help/form-settings>): Configure access, notifications, completion behavior, and other settings; some options require paid plans.
- [File uploads](<https://tally.so/help/file-uploads>): Collect files from respondents without requiring them to sign in; the free plan has a 10 MB per-file limit.
- [Payment forms](<https://tally.so/help/payment-forms>): Collect card payments through Stripe; standard Stripe fees apply.
- [Feature directory](<https://tally.so/help/features>): Find guides for form features, integrations, collaboration, and submissions.

## Help and policies

- [Help center](<https://tally.so/help>): Browse guidance on building forms, integrations, accounts, and billing.
- [Privacy policy](<https://tally.so/privacy>): Read how Tally says it processes and protects personal data.
- [Terms and conditions](<https://tally.so/terms>): Review account, publishing, use, and subscription terms.

Tally’s API is available for free.","content":"The Tally API gives developers full programmatic control over forms and submissions. Create forms on the fly, sync responses to your stack, and automate workflows, all for free. Whether you're building a client portal, an internal tool, or an automated pipeline, the API makes it possible without a single click in the UI.
The Tally developer docs are your key to a comprehensive understanding of the Tally API and help you start building quickly.
Want to use Tally with your AI assistant? The Tally MCP server lets you build, update, and fetch forms using natural language, no API calls required. It's the fastest way to manage Tally through AI tools like Claude, Cursor, or Claude Code.
- Base URL: https://api.tally.so
- Authentication: every request needs an Authorization: Bearer <token> header. Get your API key here.
- Rate limits: 100 requests/minute. Use webhooks instead of polling to avoid hitting this.
- Versioning: the API is versioned by date. Pin a version with the tally-version header (e.g.tally-version: 2025-02-01 ) so future changes don't break your integration.
- Pagination: Pagination: list endpoints (GET /forms, GET /forms/{formId}/submissions) return paginated results — pass page andlimit as request params, and check thehasMore boolean in the response (alongsidepage ,limit , andtotal ) before assuming you've got everything.
- Response codes:
| Code | Meaning | 
| 200 | Success - The request completed successfully | 
| 400 | Bad Request - The request was malformed or contained invalid parameters | 
| 401 | Unauthorized - Authentication credentials are missing or invalid | 
| 403 | Forbidden - You don’t have permission to access this resource | 
| 404 | Not Found - The requested resource doesn’t exist | 
| 429 | Rate Limited - You’ve exceeded the allowed number of requests | 
| 500 | Server Error - Something went wrong on our end | 
Wondering what you can create with Tally’s API? Here’s what our developer community has built with early access to the API:
1. Dynamic Form Creation & Customization
- Programmatically create forms
- Duplicate and personalize a form for a new client; to do so fetch an existing form's structure, then create a new one from it:
curl --request POST \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{ "status": "PUBLISHED", "blocks": [ { "uuid": "<title-block-uuid>", "type": "FORM_TITLE", "payload": { "title": "Client Intake – Acme Co" } }, ...copied from GET /forms/{formId} ] }'
status is required ("PUBLISHED", or "DRAFT"/blank for a draft). There's no name field, the API ignores it. The form's name comes from its first block, which must be a FORM_TITLE block whose payload.title becomes the form name.
2. Real-Time Form Updates
- Enable/disable fields based on business rules or time
- Dynamically change field visibility or values
- Auto-update dropdown options from live data sources (e.g. Notion, Airtable, Google Sheets); to do so pull the latest values from your source, then push them into the form's block schema:
# 1. Fetch the full form — you need every block, not just the dropdown
curl --request GET \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId} \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
# 2. Each dropdown choice is its own DROPDOWN_OPTION block, sharing a
#    groupUuid with the DROPDOWN block. Update the ones you need:
#    { "uuid": "<option-uuid>", "type": "DROPDOWN_OPTION", "groupUuid": "<dropdown-group-uuid>", "payload": { "text": "Option A" } }
# 3. PATCH back the ENTIRE blocks array — PATCH replaces the whole set,
#    so any block you leave out gets deleted
curl --request PATCH \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId} \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{ "blocks": [ ...full blocks array from step 1, with the DROPDOWN_OPTION blocks updated... ] }'
Always GET the form first and PATCH back the complete 
blocks array — partial updates will delete any block you don't include. See the Block Schema Reference for the full dropdown-option block shape.
3. Data Access & Management
- Filter and sync submissions into external tools (CRMs, dashboards, databases), to do so list new submissions and forward them downstream:
curl --request GET \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId}/submissions \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
Or use a webhook instead of polling — you'll get each submission pushed to your endpoint the moment it's created, without counting against your rate limit.
- Delete submissions programmatically
curl --request DELETE \
  --url https://api.tally.so/forms/{formId}/submissions/{submissionId} \
  --header 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
Returns 
204 on success. Deleted submissions move to Trash and follow the same recovery window as manual deletion.
Is the Tally API free?
Yes, the Tally API is free for all Tally users, including the free plan. No paid plan required to get started.
What can I build with the Tally API?
You can programmatically create and manage forms, update fields dynamically, fetch and delete submissions, and sync data with external tools like Notion, Airtable, Google Sheets, or your own database. Developers have used it to build AI agents, automated onboarding flows, client intake systems, and custom form backends.
Can I use the Tally API with Make, n8n, or Zapier?
Yes. The Tally API works great alongside no-code automation tools. Use it to create or update forms dynamically, then route submission data through your automation stack. Many users combine the API with Make or n8n to build end-to-end workflows.
How do I authenticate with the Tally API?
The Tally API uses token-based authentication. Find your API key in your account settings and include it as a Bearer token in your request headers. Full details in the developer docs.
Does Tally have webhooks or just an API?
Tally has both. Webhooks push data to your tools automatically when a form is submitted. The API gives you full programmatic control — create forms, manage submissions, update fields, and more. Many users use both together.
Can I create forms programmatically and prefill fields?
Yes, you can create forms via the API and dynamically set field values, making it easy to personalise forms per user, event, or client without manual setup.
Is there a rate limit on the API? Yes — 100 requests per minute. If you're syncing submissions continuously, use a webhook instead of polling so you don't hit it.
How do I keep my integration stable across API updates? Pin your requests to a specific API version using the 
tally-version header. A consent form documents permission before using someone's information, image, or involving them in activities that carry risk or require disclosure. Consent forms help ensure everyone understands what they're agreeing to upfront, which prevents misunderstandings and protects your organization or brand from potential liability down the line.
Consent forms aren't one-size-fits-all. The type you need depends on your activity, who's involved, and what permissions you're seeking. Some situations call for detailed documentation, while others just need simple agreement. Here are the main types and when you'd typically use them.
These are for research and studies where people need complete understanding before deciding to participate. Think university research, surveys with sensitive topics, or any formal data collection where participants should understand exactly what they're agreeing to.
When you need to share someone's information with other companies or partners, these forms keep things transparent. They're particularly helpful for staying compliant with privacy laws while being upfront about how data gets used and protected.
Cover situations where you're capturing photos, audio, or video content. Whether it's for professional photography, training sessions, interviews, or marketing materials, they set clear expectations about how the content will be used and where it might appear.
Used when businesses want to post content featuring customers, employees, or event participants on their social channels. They address platform-specific considerations like how the participant would like to be identified, content duration, and which social networks will be used.
Great for podcasters, journalists, and content creators who need clear permission to quote, publish, or share interview material. They address things like editing rights and how people want to be credited.
Required when children are involved in activities beyond regular school requirements. These parental consent forms cover safety, medical information, and emergency contacts and inform parents what their child will be doing.
Perfect for hands-on experiences that involves tools, equipment, or physical activity. They gather information about respondents’ medical conditions and physical limitations while addressing safety risks and liability concerns.
Whether you need permission for recordings, data sharing, or participant activities, consent forms help you collect clear agreements. Every situation requiring consent is different and often needs more than just a simple checkbox, that's why we've created templates for the most common consent scenarios. Each template is free, ready to use, and easy to customize to fit your specific business or project.
An informed consent form helps researchers collect consent from study participants. These forms are used for academic researchers, market research companies, and organizations conducting formal studies where participants need to understand what they're agreeing to.
This type of consent form walks participants through study details step by step, covering procedures, time commitments, risks and benefits, and their rights.
The key areas covered in informed consent forms are:
- Study overview with researcher contact information
- Explanation of activities and time requirements
- Risk and benefit disclosure
- Privacy and data protection measures
- Specific consent statements that participants must acknowledge
- Digital signature
You’ll find this type of consent form is often required before starting research activities to help protect both participants and researchers because it ensures ethical standards are met and makes it clear what participants are agreeing to and how they can withdraw.
A data sharing consent form collects permission before sharing customer information with third parties. These forms are useful for companies working with payment processors, delivery services, marketing partners, or any situation where customer data needs to leave your organization to provide services.
The key areas to cover in data sharing consent forms are:
- Clear organization details and contact information
- Specific explanation of what data needs to be shared
- Who will receive the information and why
- How the third party will use the data
- Consent statements that customers must actively agree to
- Easy withdrawal process
This type of consent form clearly explains what information you want to share, who will receive it, and exactly how it will be used.  
A photo release form collects permission before using someone's image in your photos or videos. Photographers rely on these for commercial shoots with models and subjects, and stock photo companies typically require them before accepting submissions that feature people.
These forms describe exactly how images will be used, from marketing materials to social media, so everyone knows what they're agreeing to upfront.
The key areas to cover in a photo release form are:
- Contact details and identification
- Specific usage rights you're requesting
- Whether you can use their name or tag them online
- Permission for identifiable vs. non-identifiable use
- Digital signature for legal protection
You can also customize this template for location releases when shooting at private buildings or distinctive properties that need permission.
A recording consent form gets clear permission before capturing audio or video that you plan to share publicly or use in marketing materials. Content creators and podcasters rely on these for legal protection. Customer experience teams might also use them when they want to feature customer conversations in testimonials or case studies.
The key areas to cover in a recording consent form are:
- Clear explanation of what's being recorded and why
- Specific details about how the recording will be used and shared
- Confirmation that participants can stop recording anytime
- Contact information for questions
- Digital signature for documentation
This type of consent form is essential when recordings might appear in company marketing materials, on websites, or in published content. It's different from interview consent forms, which typically cover internal research while this one focuses on public use and sharing.
A social media consent form collects permission before posting photos, videos, or content featuring people on your social channels and marketing materials. Marketing teams use these when featuring customers or employees in campaigns to confirm consent and check how participants want to be identified if their likeness is used online or in print.
The key areas to cover in a social media consent form are:
- Clear explanation of how photos and videos will be used
- Specific platforms and channels where content may appear
- Whether people can be tagged or identified by name
- Confirmation that content may be edited or adapted
- Easy opt-out process for withdrawing consent
Social media consent forms work well for businesses posting customer showcases or content featuring employees, community organizations sharing member highlights, or any situation where you're capturing content featuring people that might go public. Unlike large events that typically already include consent in ticket terms, these forms give you direct permission for specific social media use.
A client marketing consent form helps service providers get permission to share client results, progress photos, testimonials, and success stories in their marketing. Personal trainers, coaches, consultants, and freelancers use these to showcase their work while giving clients control over what gets shared and how they're identified.
The key areas to cover in a client marketing consent form are:
- Clear explanation of why you want to share client content
- Specific types of content you might post (photos, messages, testimonials)
- Multiple privacy levels for each content type
- Options to be tagged, stay anonymous, or require case-by-case approval
- Personal, honest tone that builds trust
Client marketing consent forms are useful for service-based businesses that want to feature their client results over time, not just single events or photos.
An interview consent form gets permission to record and document interviews for research, reporting, or internal organizational use. Market researchers and HR teams use these when conducting studies, but journalists also rely on them for background interviews that won't be published immediately.
This form focuses on internal documentation rather than public sharing, with strong privacy protections built in.
The key areas to cover in an interview consent form are:
- Clear explanation of how recordings will be used internally
- Strong confidentiality and data handling commitments
- Emphasis on voluntary participation and right to withdraw
- Options for audio, video, or notes-only documentation
- Choice of how the person wants to be identified
- Formal consent confirmation process
Interview consent forms work well for research studies, internal company interviews, background journalism, or any situation where you need detailed documentation with privacy protections. They're more comprehensive than simple recording forms since they often involve sensitive topics or proprietary information.
A parental consent form collects permission from parents before children participate in activities, field trips, or programs outside regular requirements. Schools and camps use these for excursions and special events. Youth sports teams, after-school programs, and community organizations might also use them for activities.
This form gathers essential safety details and emergency contacts beyond basic permission. The key areas to cover in a parental consent form are:
- Complete child and parent/guardian information
- Medical conditions, allergies, and special requirements
- Emergency contact details if parents aren't reachable
- Clear activity description and associated risks
- Permission for emergency medical treatment
- Liability release and financial responsibility acknowledgment
Parental consent forms protect both the organization and ensure parents understand what their child will be doing, potential risks involved, and that proper medical information is available if needed.
A liability waiver and release form protects businesses from legal claims when customers participate in potentially risky activities. This form can be useful for personal trainers as well as adventure tour companies, retreat organizers, and workshop organizers who need protection before activities begin.
This form combines risk acknowledgment with essential participant information and emergency details.

Free for all Tally users, no coding needed","content":"Conditional logic lets your form adapt in real time based on how someone answers. Show or hide questions, skip irrelevant pages, jump to a custom thank you page, or route respondents down a completely different path — all based on their responses. The result is a smarter, shorter form that feels personal instead of generic.
Conditional logic in Tally is completely free to use. No upgrade needed, no limits on the number of conditions you can add.
Conditional logic is a versatile tool that allows you to create tailored form experiences based on user responses. Some examples of using conditional logic include:
- Progressive disclosure: Only show fields when they're needed. Use this for waiting list forms, client check-in forms, or any form where follow-up questions depend on a previous answer.
- Lead qualification: Ask progressively detailed questions and end the form early if someone doesn't qualify — no wasted time for you or them. Route high-intent leads to a specific page or redirect URL.
- Pricing calculators: Use calculated fields with conditional logic to display custom quotes, totals, or estimates based on selections — updated live as respondents answer.
- Personalized confirmation: Show a different thank you page or message based on how someone answered — useful for quiz results, NPS follow-ups, or application outcomes.
- Personality quizzes: Display the result category respondents scored highest on, using calculated fields and conditional page jumps. See how in the personality quiz guide.
Type 
/logic to add conditional logic to your form. You can add conditions on any type of input block. Click 
: next to the logic block to remove, duplicate, add new, or wrap conditions in a group.
Use the 
cmd/ctrl + shift + L shortcut to add a conditional logic block under a selected input block.
When a logic block has more than one condition, use the 
When dropdown to choose how they're combined. - When all match: every condition must be true (an AND rule). Use this to narrow down to a specific combination of answers, for example, respondents from "Germany" who are older than 18.
- When any match: at least one condition must be true (an OR rule). Use this when several different answers should trigger the same result, for example, someone who selected "Consulting" or "Freelance" as their job type.

You can also add hidden blocks to allow respondents to enter additional information before leaving the form for more comprehensive and trackable lead capture. As a result, the form creates an interactive landing page-like experience. 
When dealing with long forms, conditional logic can become more intricate and prone to logical errors. With extensive fields, conditions, and actions, it's crucial to be cautious, as even small mistakes can sneak in. To effectively troubleshoot your form, you can follow these general steps:
- Review the conditional logic blocks: Start by carefully examining the conditional logic rules you've set up for your form. Check if the conditions are linked to the correct fields and actions. Ensure that you have configured the logic correctly based on your specific requirements.
- Edit field names: Replace the default question field names with descriptive titles that accurately describe the question or information being collected. This will make it easier to identify and manage fields when setting up or troubleshooting conditional logic.
- Test your form: Before sending your form to respondents, test different scenarios. You may find it easier to spot any errors by doing several test runs and selecting different answer options each time.
- Use @ mentions to identify the specific issue: By strategically placing @ mentions before or after the conditional logic block, you create a mechanism to track the values of relevant inputs and calculated fields at specific points in the form's execution.
- Simplify to narrow down the problem: By reducing the complexity of the logic, you can isolate specific conditions or actions that may be causing the issue and focus your efforts on debugging those areas.
What is a conditional logic form?
A conditional logic form is a form that dynamically changes based on how someone answers. Using IF/THEN rules, you can show, hide, or skip questions so each respondent only sees what's relevant to them.
Is Tally's conditional logic free?
Yes. Conditional logic is available for free to all Tally users. There are no limits on the number of conditions you can add.
What types of actions can I trigger with conditional logic?
Tally supports six actions: Jump to page, Calculate a value, Make answers required, Show or hide blocks, Hide button to disable completion, and Redirect to different URLs.
Can I combine conditional logic with multi-step forms?
Absolutely. Conditional logic and multi-step forms work great together. You can skip entire pages, show different paths based on answers, and create personalized form flows.
Why isn't my conditional logic working?
The most common issues are: the logic block is placed on the wrong page, conditions reference the wrong field, or the form hasn't been tested with all answer combinations. Use the troubleshooting steps above to debug.","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_d25742b121bd66c7aa79","url":"https://tally.so/help/how-to-create-a-multi-step-form","title":"Create Multi-Step Forms | Free Form Builder | Tally Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"With Tally, you can create a single-page form or a multi step form that displays one question at a time, improving focus and boosting completion rates fast.","content":"With Tally, you can create two types of forms: a single-page form (all questions on one page) or multi-page form (one question at a time). You might have seen form builders like Typeform use one question per page. This type of form lets respondents focus on one question at a time, which can create a more conversational form experience. That’s a multi-page form. 
With Tally, you have complete flexibility over your page structure — you can add a page break after each question for a focused experience, or group related questions together on the same page. Creating page breaks is simple: just add one wherever you need it.
To create another form page, type 
/page in your form editor. An automatic page divider and title will be inserted. Respondents will see any text or content you add below the line on the new page.
If you want your form to show one question per page, you’ll have to add a new page after each question. There are no limits on the number of pages or questions per page you can have. 
If you have many questions, consider grouping a few related ones per page instead of using a single question per page, a 30-page form with one question each can feel tedious for respondents. Whichever structure you choose, enable the progress bar under 
Settings → General so respondents can see how far along they are.
You can add a Thank you page by switching the toggle next to the last page or typing 
/thank to insert one. This will be the last page respondents see after submitting the form—you can add any content there, from text to embeds.
Working on a form with 12 or more fields? A table of contents appears automatically on the right side of the form builder. Hover to expand it and jump to any page or field in one click.
Working on a long multi-page form? Click the arrow next to a page title to fold it — the page collapses to a single line, hiding all the blocks inside. From there, you can move, duplicate, or delete the whole page in one go. All the blocks inside come along with it.

Free for all users.","content":"You can use URL parameters to pass data into hidden fields in your form. This lets you include information you already have in the form URL, helping you personalize the respondent’s experience and gain more detailed insights from your results.
Hidden fields are available for free to all Tally users.
A hidden field lets you track respondents and use already collected data to personalize your forms. It’s invisible to anyone filling out a form but lets you gather and use data effectively.
Some examples may include:
- Track the traffic source of your respondent (social media, triggers on your website, or other)
- Pass on information about your respondent to your responses (like name or email address)
- Mention information in your form, such as your respondent’s name, using answer piping
- Prefill the input fields on your form
- Pass on UTM parameters to track marketing campaigns
Hidden fields are not the same as hiding a field’s visibility. 
Open your form editor and type 
/hidden to insert a Hidden field block.
Add the hidden fields you want to pass on to your form. You can add as many hidden field blocks as you like. If you want to add your respondent's name and traffic source, add two hidden field blocks and name them, for example, 'name' and 'ref'.
Finish your form and 
Publish it. Find your form’s URL in the share tab.
When you are ready to share the form, add the parameters and corresponding values to your URL before sharing the link. There are two ways to add the parameters:
- Manually: add the variable to your form URL before sharing your form.
- Automated: use any CRM system (such as Salesforce) or email automation tool (such as Mailchimp or ActiveCampaign) to populate your data, so your respondents automatically receive a customized URL with the correct data.
The first hidden field should start with 
? . When adding multiple fields, separate them with & . 
For example, if your respondent’s name is Marie and the traffic source is email, the URL would look like this: https://tally.so/r/nPA50m?name=Marie&ref=email
You will find the hidden fields and corresponding answers in the 
Submissions tab after respondents submit your form.
Read more about mentioning hidden fields in your form using answer piping. You can also add hidden fields to your redirect URL to pass information from one form to another.
To learn about using hidden fields with popular CRM systems and email automation tools, take a look at our guides:","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_8e9aaf6b346405cb077c","url":"https://tally.so/help/form-calculator","title":"Automated Form Calculations | Free Form Builder | Tally Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"Add calculated fields to your Tally forms to score quizzes, set dynamic prices, or assign lead values based on responses. Free and easy to set up today.","content":"Calculated fields let you perform automatic calculations inside your form — think pricing calculators, quiz score totals, or lead scoring, all based on respondents' answers. You can use simple numeric and text operations, or write full formula expressions for more advanced logic.
Calculated fields are available for free to all Tally users. 
Calculated fields enable you to dynamically calculate values based on respondents' answers. Here are some common use cases for calculated fields:
- Pricing calculators: Build a checkout form where the total updates live as respondents choose products, quantities, or add-ons. Feed the result directly into a payment block.
- Quiz scoring: Add points per correct answer and show respondents their final score on a thank you page. See our guide to building scored quizzes.
- Personality and category quizzes: Tally up answers across categories and route respondents to the matching result page. See our personality quiz guide.
- Lead qualification: Assign a score or status label ("Hot lead," "Nurture") based on the answers someone gives, and sync it to your CRM via an integration.
- Name and text concatenation: Combine first name and last name into a single "Full name" field, or build a custom reference string from multiple inputs.
- Conditional redirects that use a calculated field with conditional logic to redirect respondents to different pages based on their responses.
Insert a calculated field in your form by typing 
/calculated field. In most cases, it’s best to add calculated fields on top of the form.
- Name your calculated field to easily retrieve it in calculations later on
- Choose whether the value will be text or a numeric value (number)
- Then, add an initial value as a starting point of your calculation. You can type a value, leave it blank or select a value from the dropdown.
Before determining the value of a calculated field, you need to add conditional logic to your form. Type
/logic to insert it below your calculated field block. Only you can see the calculated field and conditional logic blocks, respondents won’t see them on your published form. Conditional logic allows you to perform multiple actions. When using calculated fields, you want to select the 
Calculate action.
You can perform several numeric and textual operations with the 
Calculate action:
- Add a value
- Subtract a value
- Multiply with a value
- Divide with a value
- Assign: add a text value, for example, a label or a status, to sync contacts from your form submissions with a CRM or another tool or assign a category name to respondents based on their selected answers. Respondents won’t see this information unless it’s mentioned elsewhere in the form.
- Concatenate values: combine values in one string. For example, if you have fields for first name and last name in your form, you can create a calculated field that combines the values entered in these two fields into a single ‘Full name’ field. To use this, you need to select Text when creating a calculated field.
With formulas you write a single expression to combine multiple operations in one go, instead of chaining separate logic steps. Reference any field with 
@ mentions (e.g. (@price * @quantity) - @discount) and get real-time validation as you type.
Supported operations are 
+ - * / and parentheses ( ) for grouping
| Use case | Formula | 
| Add tax (5%) | @price × 1.05 | 
| Total with quantity | @price × @quantity | 
| Price after discount | (@price × @quantity) - @discount | 
| Apply a dynamic discount % (discount set by respondent) | @price × ((100 − @discount) / 100) | 
| Apply a fixed discount % (e.g. always 20% off) | @price × ((100 − 20) / 100) | 
| Remove a dynamic tax rate from a total (tax rate set by respondent) | @total × ((100 − @tax_rate) / 100) | 
| Remove a fixed tax % from a total (e.g. always 16% VAT) | @total × ((100 + 16) / 100) | 
| Calculate a quiz score | @score_q1  + @score_q2  + @score_q3 | 
| Build a URL with text concatenation | "https://example.com/"  + @page | 
| Combine first and last name | @first_name  + " "  + @last_name | 
| Prefix a field with a label | "ORD-"  + @order_id | 
| Build an address string | @street  + ", "  + @city  + ", "  + @country | 
| Make a certificate-style text | @first_name  + " "  + @last_name  + " has completed "  + @course_name | 
Tips:
- Always use @ + autocomplete to insert a form field
- Only type manually if you want to add text or numbers that aren’t collected in the form
- Use parentheses () to control order of operations
- Wrap literal text in double quotes, e.g. "https://example.com/" + @page
Calculations on date blocks are not available yet. 
By default, calculated values are not visible in your form. You can find them in the 
Submissions tab of your form, but you can also display the calculated values in your form, use them in a payment form, or create a dynamic redirect on completion.
To mention the calculated value in your form, simply type 
@ and choose the calculated field from the dropdown menu. You can use this to show a final price, score or quiz result in your form.
If you want to calculate and display currency, add your currency symbol directly before the linked calculated field, like in the example below.
You can use a calculated field to calculate the price of your payment form and make it dynamic based on your respondents’ answers. This means the price will change based on other inputs and logic.
- Type /payment to insert a payment form.
- Choose your calculated field from the Price dropdown menu in your payment block.
- The price will now automatically update according to your respondent's answers, for example, if they select different product types or quantities.
You can redirect respondents to different websites, landing pages, or Tally forms upon form completion. For this, you’ll need to use calculated fields and conditional logic.
You can also add hidden blocks to allow respondents to enter additional information before leaving the form for more comprehensive and trackable lead capture. As a result, the form creates an interactive landing page-like experience. 
You can use calculated fields to customize the email body or recipients of your respondent or self email notifications. Learn more about dynamic email notifications here.
Can I build a calculator with Tally?
Yes, use calculated fields together with conditional logic to build pricing calculators, quiz score counters, lead scoring systems, and more. Calculated fields are free for all users.
What's the difference between numeric operations and formulas?
Numeric operations (add, subtract, multiply, divide) apply one step at a time via conditional logic. Formulas lets you write a single expression combining multiple operations, e.g. 
(price * quantity) - discount.
Can calculated fields be hidden from respondents?
Yes. Calculated fields and conditional logic are only visible to you in the form editor. Respondents only see them if you explicitly 
@ mention the field value somewhere in the form.
I want to display the result on the Thank You page
Use answer piping: type 
@ on your Thank You page and select the calculated field from the dropdown. The respondent will see the final value after submission.
My calculated field always shows 0
This is almost always a placement or logic ordering issue. Check the following:
- The calculated field must be placed BELOW the questions it references. Tally evaluates fields top-to-bottom. If your calculated field appears above a question it references, it can't read that question's value yet. Move the calculated field to after all questions that feed into it.
- Conditional logic must fire before the calculated field is displayed. If you're using conditional logic to show/hide questions, make sure the logic conditions are evaluated before the calculated field block appears in the form flow.
- Test in the published form, not the editor. The editor preview doesn't always reflect real-time calculation. Publish your form (or use the preview link) to see the actual calculated result.
- Check your formula for typos. Field references are case-sensitive. Open the calculated field and confirm each @FieldName matches exactly the question title in your form.
If the score still shows 0 after these checks, try rebuilding the calculated field from scratch, sometimes cached formula state causes issues.
The form jumps to the wrong page
When combining Calculate actions with Jump to page actions, remember that conditional logic is evaluated from top to bottom. If an earlier logic block triggers a page jump, later blocks on the same page won't execute. Place all Calculate actions before any Jump to page actions.","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_7d74204bcd05c7c5bb0d","url":"https://tally.so/help/answer-piping","title":"Answer Piping for Smarter Forms | Free Form Builder | Tally Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"Use answer piping in Tally to mention respondents' previous answers throughout your form. Personalize questions, text, and thank you pages in real time too.","content":"In multi-question forms, you might find it useful to mention a respondent's answer to an earlier question. With answer piping, you can recall a respondent's answers from previous questions and insert them into later questions in your Tally form.
Answer piping is available for free to all Tally users.
Any answers you collect in your form can be mentioned to personalize the form experience. For example, after collecting a respondent’s name, you can mention it in a text block — Tally will automatically insert the answer in real time.
Try typing your name in the form below👇 
The most common use case of answer piping is to mention a respondent's name to address them personally in the form.
First, you need to ask the respondent's name to do this. In the example below, we added a short answer block by typing 
/short and adding “Your name” as the question.
Then, you need to add any welcome text below. In the part where you want to address the respondent by their name, type 
@ and select or type the corresponding input field, such as “Your name.” The form will now automatically mention the answer your respondent typed in the “Your name” question.
If the “Your name” question is not required and the respondent does not enter their name, you can add a default value by clicking on the mentioned value.
You can now click to 
Preview your form and fill out the question to test the result.

With Tally, you can change form colors, format text, add your logo, and apply custom styling.","content":"Customize your Tally form to fit your style or brand seamlessly. With Tally, you can change form colors, fonts, format text, add your logo, and more. Discover how to uplift the design of your forms below.
Customize your form 
Customization is available for free and doesn’t require any coding skills. Read on below ↓
Click the 
Customize button above your form title to open the customization options. You can choose between a light and dark theme or create a custom one.
Select 
Custom to create your own theme.  You can change the color of the form background, text, button, and accents (links, selected options, and focussed inputs) and select a font. To change colors, click on the colored square of one of the options. You can use the color palette to browse colors or type in a HEX code for a particular one.
If you want to reuse a custom theme, you'll need to save it as a form template first. This allows you to re-apply the same design choices to multiple forms. Themes themselves can't be saved independently yet.
You can choose any font from the Google Fonts library (900+ fonts) to use in your Tally forms. Simply select one from the 
Font dropdown.
You can change the page width and base font size for your entire form. You can also change the width, height and corner radius of your logo as well as the height of your cover image.
You can change the height and width of inputs, or make them full width. You can also change the background, placeholder and border color. Finally, you can also change the border width and radius as well as the bottom margin and horizontal padding.
You can change the height and width of buttons, make them full width or automatically adapt the width to your button text. You can change the button text font size and choose between center, left and right alignment. You can also change the background and text color. Finally, you can also change the corner radius as well as the vertical margin and horizontal padding.
Injecting custom CSS codes allows you to fully control the design of your form beyond the default design options. For example, you can change the color of input fields or add a background image.
Paste your code snippets in the 
Custom CSS box Tally will automatically display any design changes in the form builder. If this doesn’t happen, click 
Preview.
Highlight text to open the formatting options. You can change the text color, add highlight color, make text bold, italic, underlined, or add links. You can find our formatting shortcuts here.
To remove any highlight color and reset it back to default, select the text, open the 
Highlight color window, and press the Tx button.
To add a logo, hover over your form title and click 
Add logo. You can upload an image or a link to an image URL.
The recommended logo size is 200x200 pixels.
Add a cover image by hovering over your form title and selecting 
Add cover. You can upload your own image, link to an image URL, select a default color, or choose an image from the Unsplash library. Images from the Unsplash library are royalty-free — you can use them for private and public forms.
The recommended cover image size is a minimum of 1500 pixels wide.
Use different sizes of headings to add structure and context to your form. You can pick from three sizes of headings. Type 
/heading to see all heading options, or type /h1 , /h2 , or /h3 to instantly add one of the heading sizes. Type 
/divider to break up content in your form with a horizontal line. You can drag the line to move it. Hover over your form title and click 
Customize to edit the button colors. You will need to select the Custom option to open button design options.
To edit button text, click the 
⚙️ icon left of the button.
You can display content next to each other by using columns. Click  
⋮⋮ and drag and drop form blocks next to each other to create columns.
Add images by simply typing 
/image. You can upload your own image, link to an image URL, or choose from the Unsplash library. Click on 
⋮⋮ left of an image to open image options. These let you hide the image block and add a caption, image link, or Alt text. You can also delete or duplicate the image.
Did you know you can also add images to your multiple-choice options? Click  
⋮⋮ to open the block settings to insert images. Scroll down to enable the Image toggle. Then, press Add image and upload your own, link to an image URL, or choose one from the Unsplash image library.
The progress bar provides a clear way for respondents to understand how much of the form they have completed and encourages them to continue until the end. The progress bar only works for multi-page forms.
To enable it, click the 
⚙️ icon in the top navigation menu of your form editor to open the Settings page. Navigate to the General section and turn on the Progress bar toggle. Don’t forget to click Save changes.
To avoid confusion for your respondents, we advise you to disable the progress bar if your form contains multiple page jumps.
In the 
Share tab of your form, you can customize the Open Graph (OG) image, title, description, site name, and icon—this is what shows up when your form link is shared on social media or messaging apps.
Click 
Customize to update how your form appears in link previews. You can also choose whether to make your form discoverable by enabling the Allow indexing by search engines checkbox. Customize Link Preview is a Tally Pro feature.
Social media, messaging apps, and search engines may display outdated link previews due to caching, but these should update shortly.
WhatsApp won’t display the OG image if it’s larger than 300 KB. If that happens, try resizing the image to reduce its file size.","markdownUrl":null},{"id":"src_3a245294ac0a180377b4","url":"https://tally.so/help/embed-your-form","title":"How to Embed Tally Forms on your Website | Free Form Builder Tally X Reddit LinkedIn Instagram TikTok Bluesky Threads Question mark","description":"Add Tally forms to any webpage, Notion, or no-code platform. Choose from standard, popup, or full-page embeds and customize the look to fit your brand.","content":"You can embed a Tally form on any webpage and no-code tools like Notion and fully customize it to blend in seamlessly. There are three types of embeds available:
- Standard: embed your form as part of your web page
- Popup: embed your form as a popup on your web page
- Full page: embed your form as a full-page
Embedding forms is a free Tally feature.
Go to the 
Share tab of your published form and choose your embed type.
A preview modal will open with embed options. You can configure the embed options to fit your desired look.
Get the embed code and add it to your webpage. You'll find more specific instructions for every embed type below.
Any changes you make to your Tally form will automatically update the embed. You don’t have to worry about changing the embed code anytime you make changes to your form content.
However, if you change any embed styles (for example: hiding the form title or making the background transparent) after embedding your form, you have to copy the code again and replace it on your website.
Start by adjusting the embed options explained below. Then click 
Get the code or Copy embed link and add the link or code to your website.
Your website provider will generally have an option for injecting code, but it may be a feature that requires a plan upgrade.
- Height: adjust the height of your form by adding the preferred height in pixels.
- Dynamic height: automatically adjust the height of the embed to fit the form content. This will make sure the full form content will be displayed without a scroll bar. You may find it useful to make the embed height responsive between form pages and both on mobile and desktop.
- Hide form title: toggle this option if you don't want to display the form title on your website.
- Align content to the left: embedded Tally forms will be displayed in the center of your website by default. Use this option to align the form content on the left of your screen.
- Transparent background: remove the default white background to make your form blend into your website.
- Custom domain: to apply custom code injection (styles or scripts) to the embed, paste your custom domain form URL in the Custom domain field. This is a Tally Pro feature.
- Remove Tally branding: remove the Tally branding from your forms. You’ll have to upgrade to Tally Pro to unlock this feature.
Use a full page embed if you want your form to cover the full page of your website. Start by adjusting the embed options explained below. Then click 
Get the code and copy and paste it into your web page's HTML.
- Transparent background: remove the default white background to make your form blend into your website.
- Custom domain: To apply custom code injection (styles or scripts) to the embed, paste your custom domain form URL in the Custom domain field. This is a Tally Pro feature
- Remove Tally branding: remove the Tally branding from your forms. You’ll have to upgrade to Tally Pro to unlock this feature.

And the best part is you can set it up in seconds and connect to all your favorite tools.
Popup forms are available for free to all Tally users.
Start by creating a form and publishing it. You can start from scratch or choose one of our pre-made templates.
Click to 
Publish your form. Then, go to the Share tab and select Popup.
The configuration panel lets you edit your popup options, and on the right, you will get a preview of how your popup will look like.
If you close the embed panel before copying the code, you will lose your selected embed settings. Whenever you change popup options, you always need to click 
Get the code to get the latest version.
This option lets you choose when your popup form appears on your site.
- On button click: the form will appear when a visitor clicks a button on your website.
- On page load: the form will appear immediately when the page opens.
- After elapsed time: the form will appear after a specified number of seconds.
- On exit intent: the form will appear when the visitor moves their cursor to the top bar of the browser window (not supported on mobile).
- On scroll: the form will appear when the visitor has scrolled a specified % down the page.
Opening the popup on exit intent is not supported on mobile devices.
Choose whether to display your popup in the bottom right corner or the center of your website.
Want to display your pop-up in the left corner? You can do this by adding this CSS code snippet to your website (where you embed the popup).
<style>
.tally-popup {
	left: 20px !important;
	right: auto !important;
}
</style>
You can change the width of the popup by adding the desired width in pixels.
You can choose to hide the form title in your popup.
Use this option when you want to align the content of your popup to the left. This is especially useful when you increase the width of your form.
Add a dark overlay over your website content to increase the visibility of your popup.
Add an attention-grabbing emoji to your popup, and choose from our list of animations. Just type an emoji, and check the preview to see the animation in action. To open up the emoji keyboard, use these shortcuts:
- On Windows: Press win +. or right-click in the field and selectEmoji
- On Mac: Press cmd +ctrl +space
After a respondent submits the popup form, you can configure the number of seconds before the popup closes automatically. If you want the popup to close immediately after form submission, choose 0 seconds.
Turn this option On if you want your visitors to see the popup only once. However, if they clear their browser cache or open your page on another browser, they’ll see the popup again. 
Enable this option if you want your visitors to see the popup only until they submit the form. Once they’ve submitted it, the popup won’t show afterwards.
You can fully control the design of your forms with the design options available in the form builder. Read more about Tally’s customization options here.
Forms hosted on a custom domain can be customized by injecting Custom CSS or using the code injection box. Afterwards, paste your custom domain form URL in the 
Custom domain field. Adding a custom domain is a Tally Pro feature.
There are several ways you can add a popup to your website. You can simply copy the embed code and add it to your website's HTML code, or as a developer, you can use JavaScript.
- Click Get the code after configuring your popup and copy the embed code.
- Paste the copied snippet below in your site's HTML head section.

- Copy and paste the generated snippet into your website's HTML head section.
- Add the custom `data-tally` attributes to the button or any other clickable element by pasting them from the embed.
Alternatively, if you can’t modify the button's HTML, you can open the popup by adding a link with a custom URL to text or a button on your site.
